rationale: A wins because it keeps the caveats on the table without decorating the facts. Its strongest line, “Khan Academy says its AI tutor added weeks of learning — by its own yardstick,” is exactly the honest evidence story here. B is useful, but “while the rest of ed-tech charges per seat” and “one of the largest AI-tutoring deployments” smuggle in unsupported market context; that is how a decent pitch gets turned into reporter bait and then eaten alive.
gaps_in_A: “As Khanmigo scales, Khan Academy answers the independent-thinking critics directly” overpromises slightly. The update says educators question the effect on independent thinking; it does not say Khan has answered them yet.
“AI tutoring is about to reach a million more public-school students” assumes all 30 districts are public-school districts. Likely, but the supplied fact only says US school districts.
The classroom-human angle is refused as “hallucinated_fact,” which is defensible, but A could have framed it as a proof-gated regional angle instead of throwing it out entirely.
gaps_in_B: “one of the largest AI-tutoring deployments” is unsupported. The update gives 1 million additional students, not a ranking against other deployments.
“while the rest of ed-tech charges per seat” is invented category positioning. No competitor pricing or market norm appears in the update.
“The prevailing optimism — AI tutoring boosts learning” is a little too neat. The facts say Khan’s internal measure found extra weeks of learning; that is not the same as a prevailing market belief.
“landing in named districts” asks the right proof question but states the missing piece too confidently. No district is named in the supplied update.
